title: The Pair Test - a computerised measure of learning and memory
author: Sarah Buck

steps_raw.instruction: UCL INSTITUTE OF CHILD HEALTH SECTION ON COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE & NEUROPSYCHIATRY The Pair Test Administration and scoring manual Correspondence: Dr Sarah Buck Sarah.Buck@ucl.ac.uk Authors: Sarah Buck, Filipa Bastos, Torsten Baldeweg, Faraneh Vargha-Khadem LONDON’S GLOBAL UNIVERSITY

Background The contribution of neuropsychological evaluation to the diagnosis of memory impairment in patients with temporal lobe pathology is to 1) characterise the status of memory impairment in relation to other cognition abilities and 2) relate the selective deficits in memory to the neural systems subserving the mnemonic functions. However, available standardised tests do not allow comparable investigation of separate memory processes, for example between recall and recognition, hampering on the specificity and precision of the diagnosis. More balanced and controlled paradigms are required to investigate memory impairments in patients with pathology in the temporal lobes. The Pair Test offers more controlled comparisons between measures, allowing to disentangle im pairments in different memory processes in patients with known or suspected pathology in the temporal lobe. The advantages of the Pair Test are 1) a balanced paradigm allowing comparison between learning and memory measures, 2) assessment of learning, dela yed recall and recognition using one tool, 3) paired -
associate learning tool to assess cognitive processes that are dependent on the hippocampal network, and 4) the use of a tablet -based application allowing controlled administration process and engaging a pproach to neuropsychological testing. The test provides behavioural evidence of the integrity of the hippocampi and its interaction with the neocortical learning system . Overall, the test offers improved diagnosis, with more precise indication on the nature of the memory deficit and the underlying processing impairment. Components of the Pair Test The “Pair Test” is composed of analogous tasks, with relevant variables being controlled for (i.e. modality of presentation, item material, and access to semantic representations). Moreover, the tasks are equivalent in complexity and, as such, can be directly compared with each other to establish the specificity of memory impairment and provide a clearer understanding of memory deficits in brain -damaged patients. The Pair Test is a tablet-
based Application (Figure 1), with the advantage of (1) providing a controlled administration process, (2) facilitating the administration in different contexts, and (3) increasing motivation and engagement of participants as a result of the interactive platform. Figure 1. Interface of the Pair Test (version A) The five analogous tasks assess verbal and nonverbal memory and learning, while controlling for modality of presentation (auditory versus visual) and access to semantic representations (semantic versus non-semantic). The five tasks are paired associates of written words, auditory words, written pseudowords, objects, and abstract designs (see

Table 1 for examples). Each task is composed of 10 pairs of stimuli to learn over 3 consecutive trials through encoding-cued recall cycles. A final recall trial and a f orced-
choice recognition task are administered after a 15 -minute delay. The whole battery of tests requires approximately 1 ½ hours to administer. There are two versions of the Pair Test available, allowing within-subject retest at different time points. Table 1. Example of Pairs for each subtest of the Pair Test. Task Example of pair Written words Auditory words Written pseudowords Objects Abstract designs These tasks assess different cognitive processes: learning, recall and recognition. Encoding: Each pair is presented individually for 5 seconds during which the participants are asked to click on the stimulus they prefer (Figure 2). This preference judgement allows deep encoding of the pairs, minimising inter -individual variability in e xecutive functions and controlling for concentration difficulties. This is to ensure the encoding of each pair within each task, and to use the same procedure across the 5 tasks. Cued recall: After the last pair of the list is presented, the participant is presented with the left-side stimulus of each pair and asked to draw/write the stimulus that was paired with it (Figure 3). This encoding -cued recall cycle is repeated 3 times in a row for each task to establish a learning curve for each participant on that task. Recognition: In the forced-choice recognition stage, participants are presented with the first stimulus of each pair ( i.e. the cue) and asked to pick from 3 choices the target associate that was paired with the cue (Figure 4). Setting up You will need an android tablet. This application will not work on Apple devices. Download the Pair Test application from GooglePlay. Make sure the volume is on (you should hear a music), as it will be needed for one of the tasks (i.e. The Spoken Words subtest). Use the documents “Pair Test_Record form” to score performance. Administration Interface  Enter ID (the images will be saved on the device with the ID as prefix).  Click Play. General instructions “You will complete five memory tests. They are very similar in that, for each, you will try and remember pairs of items; either words, objects, shapes, or made -up words. Some might be more difficult than others, but that is okay, just try your best!” Start task  Instructions: “You will see/hear 10 pairs of words/objects/shapes, like this example [show example], one at a time. For each pair, click on the one you prefer. There is no right or wrong answer. After a few seconds, it will move automatically to the next pair. After we have gone through the 10 pairs, you will be shown the first word/image of each pair and you will try to remember what went with it by writing it/drawing it/saying it out loud. If you don’t know, that is okay, just skip to the next pair. We will do this 3 t imes with the same items, so if it is a little difficult at first you may find it easier as we repeat the task. Then, after about 15minutes, we will come back to the task and you will try again to remember as many pairs as possible. Finally, we will finish we a multiple-choice where you will be given three options, and you will select the item that you think was matched to the presented item. We will do this with all 5 tasks”.  Do not give feedback on performance. Learning trials  Do , and one after the other, without breaks. Encoding  10 pairs (1 shown every 5 sec)  “Click on the one you prefer” Recall   say out loud (see scoring sheet!)   write on canvas   write on canvas   draw on canvas   draw on canvas

 After trial : “We will do the same thing again, with the same pairs but in a different order. Again, for each pair click on the one you prefer”.  After trial : “I want you to keep these pairs in memory because I will ask you to remember as many as you can in about 15 minutes. In the meantime, we will start another game.” Delayed recall  Instructions: “Now we are going to go back to the [words/pseudowords/shapes/objects] from before. Can you try and remember as many pairs as you can?”  Delayed recall 15 minutes after the end of the learning trials ( ) for that same task.  If 15 minutes have not gone by since the end of the learning trials, then have a small break. Recognition  Instructions: “The item on the top was the one that was presented on the left earlier. I want you to try and find the item that was paired with the one on top, by selecting your answer out of the three options below”.  Do the recognition task right after the delayed recall task  3 choices, click on your response  Recognition for the auditory words is a little bit different o Instructions: “Click on each fish to hear the word they each have to say. Listen to the 3 possibilities before you make your choice. Click and hold on the fish to select your answer, you will then hear a *bip* which means that you have moved on to the next pair”.

Order of administration To avoid interference, the tasks should be administered by alternating between verbal and non-verbal materials. The delayed recall and recognition should be done 15min after that time.

Scoring Please find below a step-by-step description on how to score the performance on the Pair Test. An example of a completed record form is provided below, with the corresponding letters to guide through the steps. 1. Score each answer referring to the answer sheet (Version A or B). a. Correct b. Incorrect – 5 types of errors: i. DK: no answer is provided ii. Semantic: the answer is semantically related to the target answer e.g. “house” for “home” iii. Form: the answer is looks/sounds like the target answer e.g. “mouse” for “mouth” or for iv. From list: the answer is another item from the list, but not the target answer (refer to the document “Full list of pairs”) v. Other: a new item, invented by the participant 2. Calculate the average learning score. This is simply the average across all three learning trials, for each task separately. There is a dedicated box for this score, underneath each scoring table. 3. For each task, transfer the number of errors, in the “types of errors” table found in the record form 4. Convert raw scores to composite scores (index scores) Write the raw scores, for each subtest, in the corresponding tables. Do this for learning, recall and recognition:  Learning: average of the three learning trials  Delayed recall: score at delayed recall  Delayed recognition: correct response minus familiar and new errors (C-F-N) Then, times those numbers by 10 and write them in the composite score boxes. Finally, calculate the composite scores by taking the average of the corresponding raw scores. 5. Convert composite scores to standard scores Refer to the standardisation tables to convert raw scores into standard scores . Do this for learning, recall and recognition. Do this also for the general scores (general learning/recall, general recognition, general memory scores).  General learning/recall: average between general learning composite score and general recall composite score (across all tasks).  General recognition: general recognition composite score (box C)  General memory: average between general learning composite score (box A), general recall composite score (box B), and general recognition composite score (box C).
